The show, which opened on Sunday night at thePershing Square Signature Center, directed by Todd Kreidler, is a genial ramble through Wilsonâs early days, and through the streets of the Hill District in Pittsburgh, where his plays â the American century cycle â were mostly set. We see through Wilsonâs own eyes how the neighborhood, and the history deeply embedded in it, shaped his worldview, alternately toughened and tried his spirit, and ultimately inspired his majestic investigation of the black experience.
That the legacy of racism remained on his mind throughout his life (Wilsondiedin 2005) is established in the showâs slightly lecturely opening moments. After stepping onto the worn wooden platform of David Galloâs evocative set, Mr. Hudson hangs up coat and hat, turns a friendly eye on the audience, and then zeros in on the hard fact of slavery and its centrality to American history.
âMy ancestors have been in America since the early 17th century,â he says, âand for the first 244 years, we never had a problem finding a job.â The dark laughter this inspires is cut short when he goes on to say, âBut since 1863, itâs been hell. Itâs been hell because the ideas and attitudes that Americans had toward slaves followed them out of slavery and became entrenched in the nationâs psyche.â
Those attitudes â that blacks were âsubhuman,â âlacking in moral personality,â âlazyâ and âshiftlessâ â followed the descendants of the liberated slaves north during the Great Migration, when Wilsonâs own mother moved from North Carolina to the Hill District in 1937. The neighborhood was already an âamalgam of the unwanted,â with various minority groups living in uneasy proximity. When the local monsignor announced, one Sunday in 1955, that blacks would forthwith be welcomed at the Catholic church, it was empty a week later, save for three elderly women.
These and more brutal firsthand brushes with the racism ingrained in American culture forged in Wilson a powerful need to face down racism whenever he could. âHow I Learned What I Learnedâ hits its jaunty stride when Wilson moves beyond generalized ideas about the oppression of his people and digs into the specifics of his own life.
He dropped out of school at 15 but was a fiercely dedicated autodidact, who learned by feasting on literature and by hanging around a group of local writers and artists who were mentors and inspiration. At the same time, he had to make a living, and his tales of getting and quitting jobs reveal the streak of stern pride â or rather moral rectitude â that had already grown strong inside him.
On his first day in training at a toy store stockroom, the owner admonishes him not to steal anything; he promptly quits. When he gets a job mowing lawns, and the companyâs owner accedes to a womanâs desire not to have a black man cut her grass, he quits again. (He learned that âsomething is not always better than nothingâ from his mother, who once won a new washing machine in a contest, but refused the prize when the sponsors tried to fob off a used one on her.)
Grim though these tales often are, they are related not with bitterness but with sardonic humor. Mr. Santiago-Hudson, who appeared in the original Broadway productions of WilsonâsâGem of the OceanâandâSeven Guitars,âand has directed several of his plays, embodies Wilson with an ease surely born of longtime friendship, or at least professional intimacy. His silk-smooth voice and warm presence help animate the evening, so that even when the stories seem haphazardly assembled (or, on a few occasions, trivial), the flow of the narrative is held together by his focused, fully engaged performance.
As Wilson moves through reminiscences about an early romance with a married woman (it ended when her husband showed up at a bar with a gun), or the humbling experience of being locked up in jail for not paying his rent, a clear portrait of the striving young writer emerges: street smart but book smart, too, grateful to the men and women who inspired or helped him, but also prone to the follies of youth.
